claims.text: At stage-4 Payments does not sign invoices yet: there are no invoices and no HSM, only the InvoiceSigning sample and ADR 0015 ('will soon sign' in the situation is the ADR's plan).

The payment company's (gateway's) API key, a value it issued and can cancel and replace, reaches Payments from the Secret 'payments' (envFrom, Gateway__ApiKey) kept as a SealedSecret per ADR 0006; Program.cs line 105 sends it as a Bearer header.
claims.source_hint: deploy/gitops/config-repo-kustomize/base/payments.yaml lines 61-64; DonHang.Payments/Program.cs line 105; ADR 0015 lines 25-26 @ stage-4

claims.text: A copy of a private key produces signatures that verify exactly like the original's; a signature carries nothing identifying which copy made it. Old invoices still check against the old certificate, so the copy's signatures check too.
claims.source_hint: FIPS 186-5 ECDSA (signature depends only on key, message, nonce); ADR 0015 lines 15-16, 47-49 (old invoices check with old certificate); backend.l4.signing-documents summary line 3

claims.text: An HSM (hardware security module) creates private keys inside itself, signs on request, and can keep a key from ever leaving it (non-exportable), so callers receive signatures, not the key.
claims.source_hint: glossary hsm; ADR 0015 lines 29-31; NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 (cryptographic module, key protection)

claims.text: The Sealed Secrets controller turns a SealedSecret into a plain Secret; a Pod reading it via envFrom gets the value at start, so the key's bytes sit in the process's memory; anyone who reads that Secret has the key.
claims.source_hint: devops.l3.sealed-secrets summary lines 1, 3; devops.l3.secret-rotation summary line 5; ADR 0015 lines 25-28

claims.text: The HSM signs whatever a permitted caller sends: it knows who is calling, not which orders are paid. Stated as ADR 0015's position (line 39), not as a documented general HSM property.

With the HSM, an attacker in Payments can get signatures until the flaw is fixed and the credential Payments uses to call the HSM (its ServiceAccount, ADR 0023) is replaced; unlike a copied key, that credential can be cancelled at its issuer.
claims.source_hint: ADR 0015 lines 25-28, 35-37; ADR 0023 line 28; k8s docs service-accounts.md (token invalidation, expiry)

claims.text: Payments' own limit (sign only invoices of orders its data marks as paid, record each request) blocks bugs and wrong messages but not an attacker who controls Payments and skips the check.

ADR 0015 options: SealedSecret read at start (no new component, same as gateway key under ADR 0006; key in Payments' memory, copyable by whoever takes Payments or reads the Secret) vs HSM only Payments may call (one more component to run or rent); decision: HSM.

ECDsa is the .NET object holding the key pair; InvoiceSigning.NewKey() creates one in memory (nistP256), lab-only; Sign calls SignData with SHA256, the hash function; SubjectPublicKeyInfo is the format a certificate stores a public key in.
claims.source_hint: .NET 10 API reference: ECDsa, ECDsa.Create(ECCurve), ECDsa.SignData(byte[], HashAlgorithmName), ExportSubjectPublicKeyInfo; RFC 5280 SubjectPublicKeyInfo; InvoiceSigning.cs lines 28-38

claims.text: ADR 0015 consequences (lines 45-54, outside the excerpt): no invoice key in repo, Secret or service memory; key not exportable so losing the HSM loses the key, then new key + new certificate and old invoices still check with the old certificate; sample key lab-only; no HSM at stage-4.
Where the HSM runs (own hardware or the hosting provider's service) follows from where the system runs (ADR 0022, managed Kubernetes); ADR 0023 makes that choice (the provider's HSM service).

To sign with a software key (file or Secret), the process must hold the usable (unlocked/decrypted) private key in memory; a password-protected key file therefore also needs the password available to the service.
claims.source_hint: .NET 10 API reference: ECDsa.ImportEncryptedPkcs8PrivateKey (password needed to import before SignData)

claims.text: Trade-offs: password key file and SealedSecret both give the attacker the key, which keeps signing after the fix; HSM gives only the ability to ask, ending once Payments' HSM credential is replaced; it costs a component, and a lost HSM means a new key and certificate.

A SealedSecret can suffice for a key cancellable at its issuer (gateway API key: issue a new one, old calls lose value); an HSM for documents outsiders verify for years; a second signer or an outside party's own certificate reopens ADR 0015.
ADR 0015 justifies the HSM by custody and names its cost as one more component to run or rent (line 31, in Vietnamese; the lesson paraphrases it); it says nothing about speed.

At stage-4, git grep -n "NewKey()" gives 1 match in samples/DonHang.Samples/Samples/Security/InvoiceSigning.cs and 7 in samples/DonHang.Samples.Tests/InvoiceSigningTests.cs, none under DonHang.Payments. Run in this session.
Encryption at rest protects Secrets in etcd, but reads through the API server still return values to anyone RBAC allows.

A signature carries no trusted time: a holder of a copied key can sign an invoice showing any date, so with a SealedSecret every invoice carrying that key's signature is suspect, whatever date it shows, including future ones.
claims.source_hint: ADR 0015 lines 15-16; FIPS 186-5 ECDSA (the signature covers only the signed bytes)
